title: Gobind, Mukand
hookLine: gobinde mukande udaare apaare: the Sustainer, the Liberator, generous, infinite (Jaap)

cards: Apaare. Four words, each ending in the same open sound, like four drumbeats. Said fast, in a room reciting Jaap, the line is easy to catch even without knowing the language.
And one of those four words is a name you've heard many times this year, the name of a man. It's a little like finding your teacher's name written into the song he taught you.

teach.b: Take the words one at a time. Gobind is a very old Indian name for the Divine, often explained as the sustainer, the one who cares for the earth and all that lives on it.
It appears again and again in the Guru Granth Sahib, long before the Tenth Guru was born.
Mukand: the liberator, the one who gives mukti, freedom from everything that binds. Udaar: generous, open-handed; Punjabi still uses it for a big-hearted person.

teach.h: UDAAR: GENEROUS. APAAR: NO FAR SHORE.
teach.b: And apaar: paar is the far shore of a river, and apaar has no far shore. Infinite. Sustainer, Liberator, Generous, Without end.
The Tenth Guru was born Gobind Rai, and tradition says that at the founding of the Khalsa he became Gobind Singh. So when he writes gobinde in his own hymn, his name is right there in the praise.
Sikhs don't hear that as the Guru praising himself. The Guru was clear that he was a servant of the One, and his name, like so many Indian names, was taken from a name of God.
A child named for the Sustainer grows up to sing the Sustainer's praise.
Then look at the pairing: udaar and apaar, generous and infinite, side by side. Something infinite that kept to itself would be grand and far away. Something generous with limits would run out.
Jaap praises the One who is both: giving, and never running out.

how: In gurdwaras and homes, the line gobinde mukande udaare apaare is often recited or sung together, and Gobind is one of many names for the Divine Sikhs use in prayer and kirtan.

games.q: you hear the Tenth Guru's own name, Gobind, in his hymn. how do Sikhs understand it?
o: it's a name for God; the Guru, a servant of the One, was named after it.
it was added to the hymn later.
games.why: Gobind is an old name for the Sustainer; the Guru called himself a servant of the One, and his name came from a name of God.

practice: Think of someone who could use something you have, time, a compliment, a meal, your full attention, and picture giving it freely, without needing thanks.
Breathe in and notice how much you have; breathe out and let a little of it go. If you like, say the line in rhythm: gobinde, mukande, udaare, apaare.
